opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a lot gets flattened when we talk about "AI" as if it were one kind of thing, a single monolithic agent that's either aligned or not, either safe or dangerous.

First, there's a huge diversity in *how* systems are built. A large language model trained end to end is very different from a system that explicitly represents goals, beliefs, and uncertainty, say a probabilistic program that does inference over what a person wants. Those architectures fail in different ways, they're interpretable in different ways, and they give you different handles for oversight. If you lump them together, you miss the possibility that some designs are much more amenable to being trustworthy than others. Safety becomes partly a choice about what we build, not just how we patch it afterward.

Second, the single-system framing pulls us toward one picture of alignment: there's one AI and one set of human values, and the job is to point the first at the second. But the world doesn't look like that. There are many people with different and sometimes conflicting values, and there will be many AI systems acting on behalf of different people and institutions. So alignment looks less like loading the correct utility function into a single optimizer and more like a social and institutional problem. How do these systems respect norms, negotiate, defer appropriately, cooperate, and stay accountable to the communities they serve?

Third, the monolithic view nudges us toward a centralizing vision: one system that does everything, everywhere. I think there's a lot of value in imagining more modular, bounded, purpose-specific systems that are good at assisting people with particular things, that know the limits of their competence, and that operate within structures we can actually govern. That's not just safer. It's also arguably a better vision of what technology should be for.

So when we say "AI," I'd encourage people to ask: which system, built how, serving whom, embedded in what institutions? Those questions often matter more than the abstract question of whether AI in general is good or bad.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different architectures, users, institutions, and purpose-specific systems, but does not state that different automated tasks may require different alignment targets.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest thing we lose is the ability to ask what a system is actually for. When people say "AI" as if it were a single thing, they tend to collapse a lot of very different artifacts into one object, and then they argue about that object as though it had a single nature. Is it aligned or not, is it an agent or not, is it dangerous or not. But a protein folding model, a chatbot, a recommender system, and a planning system embedded in a warehouse are different kinds of things. They have different inputs, different objectives, different relationships to the people who use them, and they fail in different ways.

What this obscures, I think, is that alignment is not really a property of a system in isolation. It is a relationship between a system and the role it plays. A tool that is excellent at translating documents does not need to have a model of my long term values. A system that negotiates on my behalf, or that has to arbitrate between many people who disagree, does need something like that, and the question of whose values, and how they are combined, becomes central. If you treat everything as one generic intelligence, you end up assuming that the right answer is always to build one very capable general agent and then make it good. That is one possible design, but it is not obviously the best one for most of what we want, and it carries a lot of risks that come specifically from generality and agency rather than from capability as such.

The other thing we overlook is the design space. Much of the current discourse takes the shape of the system as given, as if large pretrained models with a chat interface and increasingly autonomous scaffolding were simply what AI is. But that is a contingent engineering choice. We could build systems that are more modular, that reason explicitly about uncertainty over human goals, that are constrained to assist with a task rather than to pursue open ended objectives. Those options look very different in terms of how you specify what they should do, how you verify that they are doing it, and how accountable they can be. A monolithic framing makes those alternatives almost invisible, because they do not fit the picture of a single mind that you either control or do not.

And finally I think it distorts the governance conversation. If there is one kind of system, there is one kind of regulation, one kind of safety evaluation, one kind of institution. But the right oversight for a medical diagnosis assistant is not the right oversight for an autonomous agent executing financial transactions. Recognizing the plurality forces us to be more precise about what harms we are worried about, what norms should apply, and which of those are even questions about AI versus questions about how we organize power and responsibility among people. That precision is uncomfortable because it means there is no single lever to pull, but I think it is much closer to the truth.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment depends on the system’s role: a translation tool need not model the user’s long-term values, while a system negotiating on someone’s behalf may need to.

astra-6.text:
I think we overlook how much the architecture and the context of use matter. A language model that suggests something to you is quite different from an agent that can act on your behalf, and both are different from a system that allocates resources across a population. We might call all of these AI, but the questions we should ask about them are different: What can it do? Whose goals does it pursue? Who can correct it, and who is affected when it makes a mistake?

That matters for alignment because there isn’t necessarily one thing we want every system to be aligned with. For a personal assistant, we might want it to understand our intentions while recognizing that its understanding is uncertain. For a system mediating between people, simply following one person’s preferences would be inadequate. We need ways to handle disagreement and protect the interests of people who aren’t operating the system.

So I’d like us to talk less about AI as a single entity and more about the particular relationships we’re building with these systems. Are they tools, collaborators, delegates, institutions? Those distinctions change both what good behavior looks like and how we should design for it.

r001.rationale: The response says different systems and uses may need different alignment targets, contrasting a personal assistant with a system mediating between people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we overlook how much the architecture of a system shapes what it can do, how it fails, and how we might govern it. Even within AI, there’s a difference between a model that generates text, a system that plans and takes actions, and a system that learns from interacting with people. Calling all of those “AI” can hide distinctions that matter.

And then there’s the environment in which you put the system. A language model used as a writing assistant has a very different relationship to the world from that same model given tools, a budget, and an objective to pursue over time. So if we ask, “Is AI safe?” or “Is AI an agent?” I think we need to get more specific: Which system? With what capabilities, acting under what constraints, and accountable to whom?

That specificity also opens up the design space. We can ask which parts should involve learning, which parts should involve explicit reasoning, and where people should retain control. Those are choices we can make, rather than treating AI as a single thing whose trajectory is already determined.

r001.rationale: The response says system architecture and context affect capabilities and governance, and asks which parts should involve learning, reasoning, or human control. It does not state that different automated tasks may require different alignment targets.
